tiers: Direct. The seven firms with the highest overlap score; ties go to the higher financial-services score, then to the firm closest to our size. Each profile shows its score and a one-line reason. Full profile, battlecard, weekly checks.
Adjacent. The same buyers or the same model, but not both, or a very different size: a mobile or product studio, an insurance-platform consultancy, a large IT group. Profile and monthly checks.
Reference. Firms we rarely meet but learn from: listed bellwethers for demand and price, and specialists whose strategy is worth studying. Quarterly look.
Alternatives a buyer has without any of us: hiring in-house, contractors through staffing firms, offshore integrators, doing nothing. Tracked as patterns, not profiles.
Once five or more deals against a firm are decided, tier 1 becomes the seven firms highest on the threat index (Head-to-head), re-set every quarter.
grades: Official: the company's own website, press release or filing (annual report, KRS financial statement, Companies House).
Reported: independent press, rankings (ITwiz, Deloitte Fast 50), review sites (Clutch), job boards, LinkedIn bands.
Estimate: our judgement from the evidence, such as a rubric score or a placement on the map. Always labelled.
Every value shows the date of its source. Anything older than 18 months is flagged and is not treated as current. Headcount and Clutch are re-checked monthly; revenue yearly when filings appear.
fs: Financial services is not mentioned, or is one logo among many.
One industry among several, with one or two case studies.
One of the two or three industries it leads with, or 30%+ of reviewed work, with several named financial clients.
Financial services is the identity: all of the positioning or most of the revenue, its own products, or core-platform partnerships.
model: Mostly people by the month: staff augmentation, contractors, team leasing.
Team extension and dedicated teams lead; some projects with an agreed scope.
Product development with delivery responsibility leads; team extension is a second line.
Sells outcomes: consulting-led programmes, managed services, fixed-scope products or its own software.
ai: AI appears as a skill, a technology or blog topic.
A named AI service line with its own pages and case studies.
AI is the headline: the homepage leads with it, AI-accelerated delivery is sold as the model, or the firm sells its own AI products or accelerators.
impact: Changes how we compete for banks, insurers or fintechs in the UK, DACH, the Nordics or Poland: a tier 1 firm buys a specialist, opens in one of our markets, changes its price model, or launches the same offer as ours.
A real change in offer, positioning, scale, ownership or leadership at a tier 1 or 2 firm, outside our core.
General news: awards, content, events, normal hiring, results in line with the market.
overlap: Same buyers: the financial-services score (0–3) scaled to 30 points.
Same way of selling: closeness to us on the map's people-to-outcomes axis, 30 points when level with us, none at six steps away.
Same markets: 5 points for each of the UK, DACH, the Nordics and Poland the firm targets.
Similar size: 20 points under 500 people, 12 under 2,000, 5 under 6,000, none above; 10 when unknown.
The score shows who is likely to meet us in a deal. It does not say who is better.
cadence: Website changes and news for tier 1, checked automatically; a person confirms each move and writes the so-what. Owner: marketing.
Headcount, open roles and Clutch reviews for tiers 1 and 2; a one-page digest to sales. Owner: sales operations.
Patterns and positioning map reviewed with leadership; bellwether results; battlecards refreshed. Owner: CEO with marketing.
Revenue and staff numbers from KRS and Companies House filings when they are published.
The seller records competitors on the Pipedrive deal. A lost deal needs a lost reason and, if known, who won.
method.sourcesNote: Company websites (each homepage headline copied word for word on 27 Nov 2026); revenue from KRS filings via bizraport, the ITwiz BEST100 2026 tables, reports of listed firms (SEC, Warsaw Stock Exchange) and UK Companies House accounts; Clutch profiles (search snippets where the page blocked access); Polish, Ukrainian and trade press; Whitelane and ISG buyer studies; justjoin.it's public sitemap for open roles. LinkedIn was not scraped. A missing fact says Not found rather than a guess.
questions: Leaders
Where are rivals moving in financial services, and is our position still distinct? Who is growing, shrinking, buying or for sale? How are prices and commercial models changing?
Sales
Who are we up against in this deal, and how do we win? Which rivals' clients are in transition and open to a second supplier? What will the buyer ask that a rival has already answered?
Marketing
How do rivals describe themselves, and which words have stopped working? Which proof (references, certificates, reviews, research) do they publish that we do not?
collection: Automated: competitor sitemaps and news through Exa, contract awards (TED, Poland's BZP, UK Find a Tender and Contracts Finder), the KRS daily change bulletin. A person confirms each move before it shows here.
By hand: Clutch profiles, LinkedIn headcount (looked at, never scraped), open roles on justjoin.it and nofluffjobs.
KRS financial statements, Companies House accounts, the ITwiz BEST100 tables (July).
Scraping LinkedIn, Clutch or G2 against their terms; paid deal databases; anything that needs a login or a false identity.
ethics: Public sources, official registers and licensed data only.
No pretexting: we never pose as a buyer, a candidate or anyone else, and give our name and company in any conversation.
We follow site terms and robots.txt, and never get round logins, CAPTCHAs or rate limits.
We never ask rivals' staff, former staff or shared clients for confidential information.
We track companies, not people. Names appear only in business roles (a new CEO), under a documented legitimate interest.
Every value keeps its source link and date. Claims used with buyers must be checked and fair; no disparaging rivals.

briefing.title: Financial services is now the crowded middle
briefing.text: 22 of 36 tracked firms lead with financial services. Polish specialists hold the Polish bank names (PZU, PKO BP, BLIK), and larger groups now chase Nordic and DACH banks: Software Mind opened a Nordic fintech push in October, Avenga has a Swedish core-banking migration on its record.
briefing.action: Stop saying “banks, fintech and eight other industries”. Name the problems and countries where we have proof, and win references in the UK, DACH and the Nordics, where the Polish specialists have none.

briefing.title: Hours are giving way to fixed steps and outcomes
briefing.text: 16 of 36 firms now publicly sell something other than hours. Miquido moved to outcome-based billing in the UK and DACH; Future Processing sells 4–8 week milestones with a stop decision; Infinum sells teams of three to five where projects used ten to fifteen. UK buyers' complaints include suppliers “stuck in time and materials” (24%) and “reliance on staff augmentation” (23%).
briefing.action: Keep staff augmentation, and add one fixed-length, fixed-price first step plus an agreed-scope delivery option, so a buyer can compare us on more than a rate.

briefing.title: Everyone claims AI; almost nobody shows numbers
briefing.text: 20 of 36 homepages lead with AI or agents, and nearly all promise the same thing: AI speed, human control. Only Future Processing has published measured results from its own AI-assisted delivery. HTEC sells a platform that shows clients what AI saved them.
briefing.action: Measure our own AI-assisted delivery on one real engagement (time to first commit, cycle time, defects) and publish it once cleared. A plain monthly AI-savings note to clients costs nothing to start.

briefing.title: Regulated buyers ask for a file we do not show
briefing.text: 13 of 36 firms show ISO 27001, SOC 2 or DORA readiness. Our site shows none. DORA has applied since January 2025 and banks must now register and assess every ICT supplier, subcontractors included.
briefing.action: If we hold ISO 27001 or a DORA third-party answer pack, put it on the site and in every bank proposal once the claims register clears it. If we do not, it is the cheapest gap to close for bank deals.

briefing.title: Our own proof is ageing
briefing.text: We have 27 Clutch reviews and the last is from April 2025. The tier 1 median is 51; STX Next has 103 and The Software House 78.
briefing.action: Ask three financial-services clients for a review this quarter, and keep one new review a month as a standing target.

briefing.title: Rivals are in transition; their clients may want a second supplier
briefing.text: Endava is restating results under an interim CEO; Avenga and N-iX changed CEO in 2026; Software Mind's sale fell through; STX Next is private-equity owned and buying. Account teams are changing at their clients.
briefing.action: Use the vendor intelligence already in this platform to list target accounts where these firms are the named supplier, and open second-supplier conversations there, Endava's UK payments and banking clients first.

landscapeNotes: We sit in the most crowded part of the map: finance-heavy but not finance-only, selling a mix of people and agreed-scope work. The Software House, N-iX, Avenga, Software Mind and Mindera are all within a step of us.

The finance specialists to our right are mostly Polish-only (10Clouds, Neontri, Altkom, Ailleron) or insurance consultancies (Sollers). Few sell abroad at our size: Code & Pepper and Pragmatic Coders in UK fintech, Miquido in mobile banking.

Moving right means saying financial services only, everywhere. Moving up means selling agreed outcomes as well as people. The shaded corner is where both meet; to get there we need proof in our four markets, not new words.
Placement is our judgement from public pages (see Method). Challenge it: the table under the map gives the reason for every mark.
